FOR CLAT 2027
7

1st International Big Cat Summit


• India will host the 1st International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA)
  Summit from 1–3 June 2026 in New Delhi, bringing together 95
  countries for global big cat conservation.

• The summit will be held close on the heels of the Fourth India-
  Africa Forum Summit on 31 May 2026, showcasing India’s dual
  diplomatic and environmental leadership.

• Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to attend the inaugural
  session alongside heads of state and government from member
  countries.

1st International Big Cat Summit


What is the International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA)? –

• The IBCA is the first-of-its-kind multi-country, multi-agency
  coalition committed to the conservation of seven major big cat
  species found across Asia, Africa and the Americas.

• It operates as a treaty-based intergovernmental
  organisation headquartered in New Delhi.

• Prime Minister Modi first called for an Alliance of Global Leaders to
  curb poaching during Global Tiger Day - 29th July 2019.

1st International Big Cat Summit


• The IBCA was launched by Prime Minister Modi on 9 April
  2023 during the commemoration of 50 years of Project Tiger in
  Mysuru, Karnataka.

• The Union Cabinet approved the establishment of IBCA with
  headquarters in India on 29 February 2024, with a one-time
  budgetary support of ₹150 crore for five years (2023-24 to
  2027-28).

• On 23 January 2025, IBCA formally became a full-fledged treaty-
  based intergovernmental organisation and international legal entity
  after five countries (India, Nicaragua, Eswatini, Somalia and
  Liberia) ratified the framework agreement.

1st International Big Cat Summit


• The alliance focuses on the protection and conservation of seven
  major big cats: Tiger, Lion, Leopard, Snow Leopard, Cheetah,
  Jaguar and Puma.

• Of these, five are found in India in the wild: Tiger, Asiatic Lion,
  Leopard, Snow Leopard and Cheetah (reintroduced). Jaguar
  and Puma are native to the Americas and are not found in the wild in
  India.

• The Headquarters Agreement, signed on 17 April 2025 between
  India and IBCA, provides for visas, privileges and immunities to be
  extended to the secretariat and its personnel.

1st International Big Cat Summit


• As of May 2026, the alliance has 24 member countries, including
  India, Nepal, Russia, Ethiopia, Malaysia and Liberia, with 35
  countries having consented to join.

• The governance structure consists of a General Assembly (apex
  decision-making body), a Council (7 to 15 members), and
  a Secretariat headed by a Director-General.

• All seven big cat species are listed in Appendix I of the
  Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species
  (CITES) 1973 , banning international commercial trade and strictly
  regulating any cross-border movement.

1st International Big Cat Summit


• The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 provides the primary legal
  framework for wildlife conservation in India, with the tiger and
  leopard listed under Schedule I — the highest level of statutory
  protection against hunting.

• Offences involving Schedule I species are punishable under Section
  51 of the WPA with imprisonment of not less than three years
  (extendable to seven years) and a fine of not less than ₹25,000.

• India holds nearly 75% of the world’s wild tiger
  population and the largest leopard population on earth, giving
  it unique credibility to lead global big cat conservation.

1st International Big Cat Summit

Project Tiger –

• Project Tiger was launched by the Government of India on 1st April
  1973 as a centrally sponsored scheme to protect the Bengal tiger
  and its natural habitats.

• It was initially launched in nine tiger reserves covering
  approximately 18,278 sq km.

• As of 2025, India’s tiger reserves have grown to 58 covering
  approximately 82,836 square kilometres (2.3% of India’s land
  area), with the tiger population rising from an estimated 1,411 in
  2006 to over 3,000 today.

1st International Big Cat Summit


• The National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) is
  a statutory body under the Ministry of Environment, Forests and
  Climate Change,

• NTCA was launched in 2005 following the recommendations of
  the Tiger Task Force.

• It is constituted under the enabling provisions of the Wildlife
  (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 2006.

1st International Big Cat Summit


• The Global Tiger Forum is an international intergovernmental body
  established in 1994 by tiger-range countries, including India,
  to strengthen cooperation for tiger conservation across national
  boundaries.

• At the 2010 St. Petersburg Tiger Summit (Russia), tiger-range
  countries (including India, Nepal, Malaysia, Bangladesh) launched
  the Tx2 initiative – aiming to double the wild tiger population
  by 2022.

• India achieved this target four years ahead of schedule, by 2018.

1st International Big Cat Summit


• The Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve (Andhra Pradesh) is
  the largest tiger reserve in India by area, covering
  approximately 3,728 sq km.

• A key technological advancement under NTCA is the M-STrIPES
  (Monitoring System for Tigers – Intensive Protection &
  Ecological Status) application, used for science-based monitoring
  of tiger reserves across the country.

1st International Big Cat Summit


Project Cheetah –

• Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched Project Cheetah on 17
  September 2022 by releasing eight cheetahs from Namibia into
  Madhya Pradesh’s Kuno National Park (KNP).

• It was the world’s first inter-continental translocation of a
  large carnivore, bringing the cheetah back to India 70 years after
  it was declared extinct in 1952.

• On 18 February 2023, a second batch of 12 cheetahs arrived
  from South Africa.

1st International Big Cat Summit


• A bilateral Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with South
  Africa (signed January 2023) provided for 12 cheetahs in February
  2023, followed by a dozen big cats each year for the next eight to
  ten years.

• A separate agreement with Namibia covered the initial eight
  cheetahs released in September 2022.

• Prime Minister Narendra Modi named one of the Namibian cheetahs
  introduced to Kuno National Park Aasha.

1st International Big Cat Summit


• As of May 2026, the total cheetah population at Kuno is about
  57.

• In March 2026, cheetah Jwala gave birth to five cubs, pushing
  the population past the 50-mark for the first time.

• In November 2025, India-born cheetah Mukhi gave birth to
  cubs, marking the second generation of wild cheetahs born in
  India after 70 years.

1st International Big Cat Summit

Recent News –

• Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav launched the official summit
  website and unveiled the logo on 7 May 2026.

• The summit is expected to adopt the ‘Delhi Declaration’ — the
  first-ever international declaration dedicated exclusively to the
  conservation of all seven big cat species.

• It marks a new benchmark for multilateral biodiversity cooperation,
  placing wildlife conservation at the heart of global environmental
  policy.

1st International Big Cat Summit


• Heads of State and Government from IBCA’s 24 member countries
  are expected to attend the inaugural session on 1 June 2026.

• Over 400 conservationists, scientists, policymakers,
  multilateral agencies, financial institutions, corporate
  leaders and community representatives from 95 range countries
  will participate across technical sessions.

• The summit will also see two official delegates from each of the
  95 range countries.

1st International Big Cat Summit


• The summit’s guiding theme is ‘Save big cats, save humanity,
  save ecosystem’ , highlighting the fundamental link between apex
  predator conservation and planetary health.

• Discussions will cover habitat restoration, human-wildlife conflict,
  conservation financing, and the “One Health” approach linking
  wildlife, livestock and human health.

• The IBCA serves as a platform to mobilise additional countries to
  commit to the global alliance and strengthen the conservation
  agenda.

TVK and Governor’s Delay

• After the April 2026 Assembly elections, the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam
  (TVK) led by actor-turned-politician Vijay emerged as the single largest
  party with 108 seats in the 234-member House, but fell short of the
  simple majority mark of 118.

• The Congress party extended support of its 5 MLAs, taking the
  TVK-led coalition’s tally to 113 – still 5 short of the majority benchmark.
  Although they made the Govt, Governor’s role became a huge talking
  point.

• However, Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar refused to invite
  Vijay to form the government immediately, insisting on proof of majority
  support beforehand.

TVK and Governor’s Delay

Constitutional Provisions –

• Article 164(1) of the Constitution states: “The Chief Minister shall
  be appointed by the Governor and the other Ministers shall be
  appointed by the Governor on the advice of the Chief Minister, and
  the Ministers shall hold office during the pleasure of the Governor . ”

• Article 164(2) further provides that the Council of Ministers is
  collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly of the
  State.

• The Governor is the formal appointing authority, but the real power
  vests in the confidence of the Assembly.

TVK and Governor’s Delay


• The Governor’s appointment power under Article 164(1) is not
  absolute discretion.

• The phrase “during the pleasure of the Governor” under Article
  164(1) does not give unlimited power – the Chief Minister can be
  removed only if they lose the confidence of the House, not at the
  Governor’s whim.

• Governors who act in a partisan manner or unreasonably delay
  government formation invite judicial intervention, as the
  Supreme Court has repeatedly intervened in such crises.

TVK and Governor’s Delay


• If the ruling party loses its majority, constitutional demands that the
  Chief Minister resign immediately so the Governor can invite the
  leader of the majority party to form the government.

• The Governor cannot determine majority alone and that
  determination must be left to the House.

TVK and Governor’s Delay


• Karnataka (2018): Governor gave 15 days to BJP (single largest
  party) to prove majority. Supreme Court reduced floor test to 36
  hours after midnight hearing, saying excessive time encourages
  horse-trading.

• Uttarakhand (2016): Supreme Court ordered a court-supervised
  floor test on a fixed date. Entire proceedings were video graphed
  and placed before the Court. President’s Rule was suspended only
  until the vote.

• Maharashtra (2019): Supreme Court ordered an immediate floor
  test, reiterating that majority can be determined only inside the
  Assembly – not in the Governor’s chambers.

TVK and Governor’s Delay

• In 1996, Atal Bihari Vajpayee was invited to form the government as
  the leader of the single largest party (BJP with 161 seats) in the Lok
  Sabha, even though the NDA tally was 187 – far short of a majority.

• S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) – A nine-judge Bench held
  that the only place to test majority is the floor of the House, not
  the Governor’s subjective satisfaction; the Governor may invite the
  single largest party only when no clear majority exists.

• Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006) – A Constitution
  Bench ruled that the Governor’s role is limited to a “prima facie”
  assessment of numbers. Governors cannot act as the final
  arbiter of majority and that power rests with the elected members
  of the House.

TVK and Governor’s Delay


• A floor test is a vote of confidence held on the floor of the
  Legislative Assembly. Every member votes openly to decide if the
  ruling party has majority support.

• The Supreme Court has previously held that:

 ➢ A Governor cannot conduct a floor test in Raj Bhavan – that is
   the function of the Assembly.

 ➢ The single largest party is a constitutionally recognized
   claimant in a verdict, but the true test of majority is only on the
   floor of the House.

TVK and Governor’s Delay


No Confidence Motion –

•    The Constitution does not contain the words “No-Confidence
    Motion”. This procedure is derived from the parliamentary system of
    government.

• Article 75(3) (for the Union) and Article 164(2) (for States)
  mandate that the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to
  the Lok Sabha or the State Legislative Assembly.

• The Council of Ministers remains in office only as long as it enjoys
  the confidence of the majority of members in the House.

TVK and Governor’s Delay


• The first No-Confidence Motion in the history of independent India
  was moved by Acharya J.B. Kripalani against the government of
  Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru in August 1963.

• Historically, more than 30 such motions have been moved. Former
  Prime Minister Indira Gandhi faced 15 no-confidence motions
  during her tenure.

• The only government to have actually lost a no-confidence motion on
  the floor of the Lok Sabha - Atal Bihari Vajpayee government in
  1999.

TVK and Governor’s Delay


• Any member of the Lok Sabha or State Assembly can move a motion
  of no-confidence in the Council of Ministers.

• To be admitted, the motion must be backed by the support of at
  least 50 members when introduced in the Lok Sabha.

• The member who moves the motion is not required to provide
  any specific reason, the motion expresses a want of confidence in
  the Council of Ministers.

TVK and Governor’s Delay


• The Speaker has the initial discretion to examine the notice and
  decide if it meets the procedural requirements.

• If admitted, the Speaker sets a date for the debate and voting.
  According to Rule 198 of Rules of Procedure and Conduct of
  Business in Lok Sabha, the allotted date cannot exceed 10
  days from the day the motion is accepted.

• The Speaker has the power to decide on the scheduling of the
  motion, even amid political demands for an immediate vote.

TVK and Governor’s Delay


• At the end of the debate, a vote is held. The motion is passed by a
  simple majority of members present and voting.

• If members abstain from voting, their numbers are removed from the
  total strength of the House for the purpose of calculating the
  majority.

• If the motion is passed by the required majority, the Council of
  Ministers automatically loses its mandate and must resign from
  office.

TVK and Governor’s Delay

Recent News –

• The Governor asked Vijay to show proof of support from 118 MLAs
  before swearing him in. This can be seen as his right to do a basic
  check of numbers.

• But critics say the Governor is acting like he is holding a floor test
  in his own office. The Supreme Court has said this is not allowed.

• Asking for 118 letters of support goes beyond a simple check and
  takes over the role of the Assembly.

TVK and Governor’s Delay


• TVK’s own strength: 108 MLAs after the elections.

• Congress support: 5 MLAs, taking total to 113.

• TVK was in talks with the CPI(M), CPI, VCK, and IUML to shore
  up additional numbers – reportedly, support from six more MLAs was
  forthcoming.

• The Governor has refused to set a timeline for swearing-in, insisting
  that numbers be demonstrated first.

TVK and Governor’s Delay


• The CPI(M), CPI, and VCK had asked the Governor not to delay
  Vijay’s swearing-in, arguing that the single largest party should be
  invited to form the government immediately.

• The DMK and AIADMK have not formally committed to supporting
  TVK, leaving the coalition arithmetic fluid.

• The Congress has reaffirmed its support to TVK but has not added
  more numbers beyond its 5 MLAs.

Passage:

A floor test is a constitutional mechanism used to determine whether a government
enjoys the confidence of the legislative assembly. It becomes particularly important
during political instability, defections, coalition disputes, or claims by rival groups to
form the government. In India, Governors may direct a Chief Minister to prove majority
support through a floor test conducted inside the House.

The process is considered an essential aspect of parliamentary democracy because the
majority of elected representatives must support the government. Courts in India,
including the Supreme Court, have repeatedly emphasised that questions regarding
majority support should ordinarily be tested on the floor of the House rather than
decided through subjective assessments outside the legislature.

Source: The Hindu

A floor test is conducted primarily to determine:

A. Validity of elections
B. Financial position of the government
C. Majority support enjoyed by the government
D. Constitutionality of laws
ANSWER - C

A floor test generally takes place in the:

A. Supreme Court
B. Governor’s office
C. Legislative House
D. Election Commission
ANSWER - C

In state politics, a floor test is usually ordered by the:

A. Chief Justice of High Court
B. Speaker alone
C. Governor
D. Election Commission
ANSWER - C

Floor tests are a feature of which form of government?

A. Presidential system
B. Parliamentary system
C. Monarchical system
D. Dictatorial system
ANSWER - B
